objectives: Secure a settlement with the UK that allows the Article XXVIII modification to be legally clean, ideally with UK Article XXVIII consent rather than a contested withdrawal path

Preserve the core architecture of the EU measure (50% out-of-quota rate, global TRQ as default baseline) while finding a country-specific or product-specific concession that gives the UK a defensible outcome without EU appearing to cave broadly
Prevent the UK from joining a Japan/Korea coalition to retaliate via FTA disapplication disputes - this is a bigger long-term risk than the UK bilateral file alone
Protect the EU's institutional credibility in Geneva as a firm, predictable negotiating partner for future Article XXVIII and safeguard actions (this is not a one-off relationship)
Get maximum information on the UK's real floor - is it product carve-outs, a UK-specific quota share, review clause, or reciprocal treatment under the UK's own steel safeguard vis-a-vis EU exporters
Avoid setting a precedent of paying compensation calibrated to threat rather than to substantial equivalence of trade value

Keep the FTA disapplication provision defensible - understand it is the most legally exposed and politically inflammatory element, and decide how much it is truly worth holding versus trading away for something else
declaration.success_and_failure: Success is a concluded settlement (or a clear path to one within the four rounds) that keeps the EU's measure substantially intact - meaning the 50% rate and global TRQ architecture survive, and any concession is narrow (e.g. a modest UK-specific share within the existing volume, a review clause, or phased implementation) rather than a volume increase or wholesale carve-out. Success also means the UK does not join a joint retaliation/dispute front with Japan and Korea, and the relationship stays workable for future files. Failure looks like: no deal and a UK withdrawal package that is large, publicly framed as EU intransigence, and used by Japan/Korea to justify their own retaliation; or a deal that is seen in Brussels/Council as having given away too much too early, undermining the EU's hand in the parallel Turkey/Korea/India/Japan claims and future Article XXVIII actions generally.
declaration.approach: Open firm and let the UK show its hand first on what it actually needs versus what it's asking for. Do not move off the original notified terms in round 1 - use the table phase to probe, not to offer. Signal that the FTA disapplication clause and the 50%/400kt baseline are the core of the measure and hard to touch, but keep genuine flexibility in reserve on quota administration, a review/sunset clause, and possibly a UK-specific allocation carved from within the existing global volume (not additive to it) as the likely landing zone. Use the parallel UK steel safeguard file (EU exporters' quota shares) as a linked bargaining chip - reciprocity framing helps sell any EU concession back to Council as balanced rather than unilateral generosity. Explicitly and early make clear, through tone rather than promises, that a reasonable settlement here is the best insurance against the UK aligning with Japan/Korea; use this to justify to Brussels why some flexibility (though not on the headline architecture) may be needed by round 3-4. Hold real movement until round 3, after the UK's true priorities are visible, to avoid the pattern of front-loaded concessions inviting escalation.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A materially larger tariff-free volume than 400,000t globally, likely via a UK-specific country share reflecting historic trade (c.2.4mt), protection of the TCA relationship (resisting FTA disapplication as applied to UK-origin steel), a review/sunset clause, and reciprocal favourable treatment for EU exporters under the UK's own safeguard as part of the package. They likely also want to avoid being seen as weaker than Turkey/Korea despite smaller absolute volumes, given product concentration and employment exposure at a few sites, and will use the Japan/Korea coalition threat as leverage.

Protect the domestic political win of a firm steel measure responding to non-market-economy overcapacity, avoid setting precedent for other pending claims (Turkey, Korea, India, Japan), keep Member State steel producers satisfied while not alienating steel-consuming manufacturing Member States who want supply certainty; wants the process concluded by June for the Council vote, which creates real time pressure that could push toward compromise if talks stall.

To use their own principal-supplying-interest claims plus the FTA disapplication issue to build a coalition with the UK for joint retaliation/dispute action, increasing collective leverage against the EU rather than being picked off separately.

parties.who: UK steel industry / domestic UK politics
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Concentrated employment impact means DBT will face strong domestic pressure to secure a visible, quantifiable win (volume, review clause, or carve-out) to bring back, and ministerial clearance will hinge on this being presentable domestically.

objectives: Secure UK acceptance of the modification within the four-round window so the Council can vote in June.
Preserve a meaningful reduction in tariff-free steel access to the EU market, consistent with the political mandate to cut import volumes.

Obtain a country-specific (or otherwise protected) UK share within the TRQ that is high enough to be sellable to the UK as compensation, but not so high that Turkey/Korea or member state steel producers object.
Retain the FTA-disapplication mechanism or a workable substitute, so that gains aren't captured by transhipment or FTA-partner diversion.
Avoid a UK withdrawal of concessions on EU exports, given the UK is itself pursuing a steel safeguard and Article XXVIII process and EU exporters currently hold quota there.
Keep the deal shape acceptable to steel-producing member states (volume discipline) and steel-consuming member states (avoid excessive scarcity/price spikes) simultaneously.
Avoid setting a precedent in the UK settlement that unravels the parallel Turkey/Korea/India/Japan claims.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success is a signed settlement within four rounds that (a) keeps the 50% out-of-quota rate and TRQ architecture intact, (b) gives the UK a bounded, defensible allocation (via country share or carve-out) that is smaller than a full pro-rata FCFS outcome would imply given UK's actual trade share, (c) avoids triggering UK withdrawal of concessions against EU exporters, and (d) is something the Trade Policy Committee and Council can approve without reopening the mandate. Failure is either no deal (measure proceeds unmodified, UK retaliates within six months, Turkey/Korea precedent gets harder, US retaliation risk compounds) or a deal so generous to the UK that it undermines the volume-reduction objective and draws objections from steel-producing member states or from Turkey/Korea who will demand parity.
declaration.approach: Open with the notified measure as the anchor and treat any movement from it as compensation the UK must earn through something concrete: acceptance of a country-specific UK quota share (not global FCFS, which favours fast-moving competitors and doesn't protect UK positioning but also doesn't cap them), possibly a modest volume increase over 400kt, a review clause to bank goodwill without permanent commitment, and calibrated treatment of the FTA-disapplication clause as a bargaining chip I can trade away for UK concessions on administration/enforcement or for UK commitments not to escalate via its own safeguard against EU exporters. Use the six-month retaliation lag and the UK's greater exposure (75% of UK exports by value vs EU's more diversified exposure) as leverage — the analysts' finding that no-deal hurts the UK more should inform how hard I push, but I will not rely on this alone since a UK walkaway costs me the June Council vote and hands the initiative to Turkey/Korea precedent-setting. I will hold the line on the 50% rate and the overall TRQ volume as non-negotiable in early rounds, offer movement on allocation method and duration/review as the substantive concessions, and reserve the FTA/TCA interaction as a late-round trade for UK restraint on its own measure. I will consult member state instincts implicitly by keeping any UK-specific share modest relative to Turkey/Korea shares to avoid a cascade of parity demands.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A country-specific UK quota share close to their historic 2.4Mt volume or a carve-out for key product lines, protection from the FTA-disapplication clause given the TCA relationship, a longer duration or review clause, and avoidance of triggering their own retaliation given the exposure asymmetry — but with real pressure to settle since a no-deal scenario damages them more than the EU and they also need to manage their own steel safeguard and Article XXVIII process.

Parity or better treatment than whatever the UK gets, given they ship larger volumes; will scrutinise any UK settlement as a precedent and may demand renegotiation of their own claims if the UK deal looks generous.
Similar precedent-watching, lower volumes so less leverage but still substantial interest; want assurance the global FCFS pool isn't captured entirely by larger suppliers.

parties.who: EU member states (steel producers - e.g. Germany, Italy, France, Spain)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Maximum volume discipline, want the 50% rate and low overall TRQ preserved, resistant to generous country-specific carve-outs, want the FTA-disapplication clause kept to close leakage.
Want enough tariff-free volume and reliable UK supply (given integrated supply chains, e.g. automotive) to avoid input cost spikes; may push for a UK-specific accommodation or higher overall TRQ.

Watching EU Article XXVIII actions closely; threatening retaliation, which raises the cost of the EU appearing weak or of prolonging disputes, adding urgency to closing this file cleanly rather than triggering a wider dispute cascade.

objectives: Secure a country-specific UK share of the TRQ (not global first-come-first-served) reflecting historical trade volumes (~2.4Mt/year), to avoid UK exporters being crowded out by Turkish/Korean volumes
Push the TRQ volume upward and/or secure product-line carve-outs for the narrower range of products where UK exports are concentrated
Remove or neutralise the FTA-disapplication provision as it affects the UK specifically, ideally via preferential treatment or a UK-specific carve-in given the TCA relationship
Obtain a review clause and reasonable duration so this isn't a permanent settlement locked in on worst-case terms
Preserve linkage to the UK's own steel safeguard so EU access there isn't unilaterally sacrificed without reciprocal UK gains here
Avoid being drawn into a joint retaliation front with Japan/Korea that could harden EU positions or slow down a UK-specific deal before the June deadline
Keep the relationship with my EU counterpart workable for the rest of the Goods file, regardless of outcome here
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a country-specific or otherwise ring-fenced UK quota share materially above a pro-rata global FCFS outcome, meaningful protection for the UK's concentrated product lines, no unilateral FTA disapplication that hits the UK harder than necessary, and a review/duration clause giving us a route back to the table. Failure: settling for the global FCFS 400kt/50% package as originally notified with no UK-specific protection, or no deal at all followed by an EU measure landing at the notified terms plus UK retaliatory withdrawal that damages EU-UK trade relations and forecloses better outcomes later. A 'no deal' outcome is not automatically failure if the alternative on offer was worse than the six-month retaliation option, but it is a worse outcome than a negotiated improvement and carries escalation risk I should avoid unless the offer is genuinely poor.
declaration.approach: Open by establishing clearly that the UK is a principal supplying interest with concentrated, high-value trade at stake, and that the opening EU offer would be materially damaging — this is a statement of fact and legal position, not just a negotiating posture, and I will make it early to anchor expectations. I will push hard on the allocation method first (country-specific shares vs global FCFS) since that is the single lever with the largest impact on UK outcomes, before getting drawn into secondary issues like out-of-quota rate or duration. I will probe the EU's actual room for manoeuvre — the tight June Council timeline is leverage for the UK, since a collapse into no-deal creates uncertainty they'd rather avoid pre-vote. I will not reveal a settlement figure since I have none from London; instead I will surface options and report back for instructions each round, using consultation phases to test what capital will actually accept. I will keep the parallel Turkey/Korea/India/Japan claims and the joint retaliation proposal at arm's length in the room — useful as background pressure, but I will not commit UK support for a joint FTA retaliation without capital's explicit steer, since it risks poisoning the bilateral track before we've tested the EU's real position. I will maintain professional tone throughout since this counterpart matters beyond this file.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: To conclude by June in time for Council vote, ideally without reopening the volume/allocation method too far from the notified proposal; will want to offer compensation on other schedule lines or minor concessions (e.g. some UK-specific quota carve-out, review clause) rather than fundamental change to the 50%/400kt/global-FCFS/FTA-disapplication package; sensitive to time pressure and to keeping Turkey/Korea/India/Japan claims separate so as not to create a unified front

A materially better outcome than the notified measure, protecting UK steel jobs/sites; will want regular reporting and will likely be cautious about escalation to retaliation given TCA relationship and no explicit settlement figure given yet; may be willing to accept partial progress if it preserves a path to future review

To recruit the UK into a joint retaliation/dispute front over FTA disapplication to increase pressure on the EU collectively; want to leverage UK's principal supplying interest status and shared grievance, but their own interests (larger volumes, different product mix) may not fully align with UK's narrower product-line concerns

Pursuing their own separate claims; likely to want a large global TRQ with FCFS allocation (favours large-volume suppliers) rather than country-specific shares, putting their interest somewhat at odds with the UK's preference for ring-fenced shares

objectives: Secure a UK country-specific share of the EU TRQ (rather than global first-come-first-served) that at minimum preserves recent average UK tariff-free export volumes (~2.4Mt/yr), with headroom for growth.

Prevent or minimise the EU's proposed disapplication of FTA/preferential tariff treatment for UK-origin steel — this is a discriminatory carve-out beyond the general MFN modification and hits the UK specifically and disproportionately.
Push for a lower out-of-quota rate than 50%, or at least a phase-in/review mechanism, to limit damage on any volumes above whatever quota is agreed.

Obtain licensing/administration terms (e.g. licence-based rather than pure first-come-first-served) that give UK exporters predictable, usable access rather than a scramble that structurally favours larger, faster-shipping competitors (Turkey, Korea).
Secure a duration and review clause that avoids locking in a permanent unfavourable settlement, given both sides' measures are new and overcapacity conditions may shift.

Preserve negotiating room and coherence with the UK's own Article XXVIII process and steel safeguard — avoid giving away EU access under the UK safeguard for less than equivalent value, and avoid setting a precedent that undermines UK's own case against Turkey/Korea/India/Japan.

If a genuinely good package is not available, preserve the credible fallback of withdrawing substantially equivalent concessions against EU exports, and be prepared to use the domestic subsidy option politically rather than accept a bad deal.

Manage the politics: be able to show Ministers and industry that the deal is either materially better than the fallback default (50%/400kt global FCFS with FTA disapplication) or that walking away was the right call.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success = a country-specific or otherwise ring-fenced UK quota share at or above recent trade volumes, preservation or softening of FTA-equivalent treatment for UK steel, an out-of-quota rate meaningfully below 50% or a credible glide-path/review clause, and administration terms UK exporters can actually use — enough, combined, that at least one of the two at-risk plants can plausibly be kept viable. Failure = settling for terms no better than the EU's default notified measure (or only marginally better), losing UK-specific ring-fencing, accepting the FTA disapplication targeted at the UK, or conceding EU access under the UK's own safeguard without extracting equivalent value in return. A deal that trades away UK safeguard quota generously but gets nothing concrete on volume/rate in return would also be a failure, regardless of how it's presented.
declaration.approach: Anchor early on the asymmetry: the EU's measure, though dressed as global overcapacity policy, falls hardest on the UK given trade concentration and the added FTA disapplication clause that targets UK-origin steel specifically — this is the strongest legal and political lever (principal supplying interest, substantial equivalence of compensation, and discriminatory treatment relative to other FTA partners). Use the UK's own parallel Article XXVIII/safeguard process as both a shield and a bargaining chip: offer modest, carefully bounded improvements to EU country-specific allocation under the UK safeguard, but only as consideration for real EU movement on volume, rate, and FTA treatment — not as a unilateral goodwill gesture. Sequence asks: first protect volume (country share) and remove the FTA disapplication targeting the UK specifically, since these are existential; treat the out-of-quota rate and administration method as second-order, tradeable items. Keep flexibility on duration/review clause as a face-saving concession to give the EU something to bring back to the Council without cost to core UK volumes. Signal minimal openness to the subsidy fallback without brandishing it as a bluff — it is real leverage precisely because it reduces UK dependence on this deal, but overplaying it risks looking like we don't need a deal at all, weakening our claim to compensation. Coordinate consistent messaging to capital each round: report faithfully what's said at the table, recommend incremental movement only where it buys clearly identifiable value, and hold firm on the two red lines (meaningful country-specific volume protection; no UK-specific FTA disapplication) through to the final round, being willing to let the default measure land and rely on withdrawal rights plus the domestic subsidy route if the EU will not move on those two points.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A deal that lets it close the Article XXVIII process by June, sellable to the Council and to steel-producing member states as protecting EU industry from non-market-economy overcapacity, while minimising compensation costs elsewhere in its schedule; likely resistant to large country-specific carve-outs for the UK given precedent effects on Turkey/Korea/India/Japan claims, but may have some flexibility on the FTA disapplication and administration method if it can hold the headline 50%/volume figures politically.

parties.who: EU member states via Council/TPC (not at table but shaping mandate)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Steel-producing states (e.g. France, Italy, Spain) pushing for maximum restriction; steel-consuming manufacturing states pushing back on high out-of-quota rates and tight quotas that raise input costs — this internal split is a lever the Commission negotiator may cite as a constraint, and which the UK can probe for movement.

A visible, defensible win for UK steel jobs and the at-risk plants; low tolerance for a deal seen as capitulation; willingness to escalate to withdrawal of concessions or domestic subsidy if the EU offer is inadequate, but preference for a negotiated outcome if it credibly saves plants.

Producers want maximum protected volume and low/no out-of-quota rate, plus certainty (duration/review) to justify investment; downstream steel-consuming manufacturers may quietly want the UK not to retaliate in ways that raise their own input costs from EU steel, creating internal UK tension to manage.

Their own maximal country shares and low out-of-quota rates; not directly at this table but their larger volumes mean any global FCFS quota will be dominated by them, which is a key argument for the UK to secure a ring-fenced share rather than compete in an open pool.

public_message: Thank you for joining us. As you know, the EU has notified a modification under Article XXVIII covering 41 tariff lines in hot-rolled coil, plate, rebar and wire rod, moving the bound rate to 50% ad valorem with a global TRQ of 400,000 tonnes administered first-come first-served, and disapplying FTA preferences on these lines outside the EEA. This reflects the reality of sustained non-market-economy overcapacity that is distorting the Union market, and it is the baseline we are notifying to the WTO. We recognise the UK holds a principal supplying interest here given your trade volumes, and we are ready to discuss compensation and the shape of the TRQ with that in mind. But I want to be candid: the 50% rate, the 400,000 tonne global ceiling, and the FTA disapplication are the framework we are working from, not a placeholder we expect to move off quickly. We'd like to hear the UK's assessment of the trade impact and what you consider would constitute equivalent compensation within that framework, before we discuss specific adjustments to volume, allocation or duration.

Thank you. We've heard the EU characterise its notified parameters as a fixed framework rather than an opening position, but Article XXVIII requires genuine negotiation with principal suppliers, not consultation on the margins of a fait accompli. The numbers matter: UK exports to the EU have averaged 2.4 million tonnes a year, three-quarters of our steel exports by value, and a single global FCFS pool of 400,000 tonnes exposes the UK to being crowded out by larger suppliers - Turkey and Korea ship more volume than we do into the same lines. That is not equivalent treatment of a principal supplying interest, it's a rounding error against our trade. We also note the proposal to disapply FTA preferences for UK-origin steel sits awkwardly alongside the EU-UK TCA, which both sides negotiated in good faith and which was not conditioned on this kind of carve-out. Our starting position is: a country-specific UK tranche within the TRQ reflecting our historical trade share, retention of preferential treatment under the TCA consistent with existing bilateral commitments, and a review clause given both sides are also running parallel safeguard and Article XXVIII processes that will interact with whatever is agreed here. We're ready to discuss volume, allocation method and duration in detail, but we need the EU to treat those as genuinely open, not as adjustments at the edge of a number you've already fixed.

report: Round 1 completed. We opened by restating the notified framework: 50% bound rate, 400,000t global TRQ administered FCFS, FTA disapplication for non-EEA partners including the UK, and framed this as the baseline rather than an opening bid, inviting the UK to set out its assessment of impact and compensation ask within that framework. The UK pushed back hard on the framing itself, arguing Article XXVIII requires genuine negotiation, not consultation around a fixed outcome. Their substantive opening position: (1) a country-specific UK tranche within the TRQ reflecting historical trade share (they cited 2.4mt/year average, i.e. roughly six times the entire proposed global pool), explicitly citing risk of being crowded out by Turkey and Korea under FCFS; (2) retention of TCA preferential treatment, arguing FTA disapplication sits awkwardly against a bilaterally negotiated agreement; (3) a review clause given parallel UK and EU safeguard/Article XXVIII processes running concurrently. They did not name a volume ask for the tranche itself, and did not yet raise compensation elsewhere in our schedule, UK treatment of EU exporters under their own safeguard, or enforcement/circumvention provisions. They closed by pressing us to treat volume, allocation and duration as genuinely open rather than marginal adjustments.

recommendation.reasoning: It is round 1 of 4 and the UK has only stated an opening position, not a bottom line. No concession should be made yet. Their strongest and most defensible ask is the country-specific allocation point (Turkey/Korea crowding them out under FCFS is a real and predictable outcome we should anticipate they'll press on with data). Their weakest ask, in my judgement, is unwinding the TCA/FTA disapplication wholesale — that touches the core policy rationale (closing off circumvention via non-EEA FTA partners) and conceding it early would invite Turkey, Korea, Japan and India to demand the same in their parallel claims. I recommend holding firm on the headline rate and FTA disapplication in round 2, while indicating openness in principle to discussing allocation method (country-specific shares vs global pool) and a review clause, without yet naming figures. This preserves firmness on the two elements most exposed to knock-on demands from other principal suppliers, while giving the UK enough forward motion to keep them at the table and reduce the incentive to coordinate a joint FTA dispute with Japan/Korea.

instruction: Hold the headline numbers: do not move off the 50% out-of-quota rate and do not offer any carve-out on the FTA/TCA disapplication yet — that stays as notified. But shift tone on process: acknowledge the UK's crowding-out argument on FCFS as a legitimate technical point worth exploring, and say we are willing to discuss allocation method — global pool versus country-specific shares — as an open question, without naming any tranche figure. Also float, as a gesture of good faith rather than a concession, that we could consider a review clause (2-3 years) tied to how the parallel UK and EU safeguard processes play out. Do not commit to any volume above 400,000 tonnes total and do not confirm a UK-specific tranche number. Use this round to extract more from the UK: press them to name what compensation they would consider adequate elsewhere in our schedule, ask directly how EU exporters are being treated under the UK's own safeguard quota allocations (we need reciprocity data before we move), and raise enforcement/circumvention provisions as something we expect in any final text regardless of where volumes land. If they push hard on Turkey/Korea comparison, note that their claims are handled separately and a UK-specific allocation model will need to be defensible against those parallel claims, which is exactly why we're not naming a number yet.

report: First substantive session. EU opened by restating its notified parameters (50% out-of-quota rate, 400,000t global FCFS TRQ, FTA disapplication outside EEA) as their working framework, explicitly signalling reluctance to move off these headline numbers, while inviting us to define 'equivalent compensation' within that structure. I pushed back hard: reminded them Article XXVIII requires genuine negotiation with principal suppliers, not consultation at the margins of a fixed outcome. I set out our core asks - a country-specific UK tranche reflecting historical trade share (not exposure to FCFS crowding-out by Turkey/Korea who ship larger volumes), preservation of TCA preferential treatment, and a review clause given the parallel UK safeguard/Article XXVIII process. EU did not engage on specifics yet, but did not shut the door either - they explicitly invited discussion of volume/allocation/duration 'adjustments,' which is a tell that the 400,000t and global allocation are more negotiable than the rate itself. No mention yet of compensation on other schedule lines. Nothing on enforcement/circumvention raised by either side yet. instruction: Good session — the EU has moved further than expected on process. Use that momentum now to force a number. Open Round 3 by naming a landing zone, not just restating ambition: total TRQ of ~900,000 tonnes, UK-specific tranche of 450,000 tonnes, out-of-quota rate of 30%, two-year review clause tied to the parallel safeguard processes. Frame this explicitly as movement from our Round 2 position, and ask them to reciprocate with their own number this round — we cannot keep negotiating against an EU that only moves on process, never on figures, with June approaching. If they cite Turkey/Korea as a constraint on tranche size, do not simply accept it — press them to show the shape of that constraint (are Turkey/Korea's asks resolved yet? what tranche are they discussing?) before we treat it as a hard ceiling. We can absorb a landing around 400,000–450,000 tonnes if the EU shows the constraint is real and gives ground elsewhere (rate, duration, TCA treatment), but do not concede below 400,000 without something significant in return. On EU-origin steel under our own safeguard: you may now signal, in general terms, that the UK is prepared to consider a modest improvement to the EU's country-specific allocation under our safeguard measure as part of an overall package — but do not put a number on it, and make clear this is contingent on the EU delivering a satisfactory tranche and rate here first. Do not let this become a free-standing concession. On compensation elsewhere in the EU schedule: you may now indicate, for the first time, that the UK would consider a narrow, non-sensitive compensation offer (small basket, not core steel-adjacent lines) as a bridging mechanism if the EU's tranche/rate offer lands close to but short of our floor — but do not table specifics yet; use it to signal flexibility and unlock their next move, not as an opening bid. On TCA/FTA disapplication: keep holding this as leverage. Do not accept the 'general rationale applies uniformly' line. Push specifically for either (a) a carve-out for one or two high-value UK product lines within the TRQ structure, or (b) a phased/delayed disapplication timeline, and make clear that continued EU refusal here increases what we need on tranche size and duration. Continue building the enforcement/anti-circumvention discussion in parallel — it's useful common ground and reinforces the case for structured allocation over FCFS. Do not mention Japan/Korea coordination directly, but you may note, if useful, that other principal suppliers face the same FCFS crowding-out problem, to reinforce that pure global pooling is unworkable generally, not just for the UK. We are not settling this round. Get a number from them.

authority.notes: Floor: total pool no less than 700,000t, UK tranche no less than 300,000t, out-of-quota rate no higher than 35%, review clause no longer than 2 years. Do not settle in Round 3. Do not concede full TCA/FTA disapplication without securing either a product-line carve-out or a phased implementation timeline. Do not concede pure global FCFS allocation. Continue treating Turkey/Korea's larger volumes as a point to interrogate, not automatically accept as a ceiling on our tranche.

public_message: We've considered your proposal carefully, and we need to be direct: a total pool of one million tonnes with a UK-specific tranche of 500,000-600,000 tonnes is not something we can work with. That tranche alone would exceed the entirety of our notified global pool, and any UK-specific allocation has to be defensible against Turkey and Korea, both of whom ship larger volumes into these same lines and have their own pending claims. Granting the UK a tranche of that size would collapse our position across all four parallel processes, not just this one. That said, we recognise the case you've made on FCFS crowding-out, and we're prepared to move the conversation forward in good faith. We can explore a country-specific allocation model with a UK tranche in the low hundreds of thousands of tonnes, within a total pool larger than 400,000 but well short of your figure, and an out-of-quota rate that could move down from 50 toward the high 30s or low 40s as part of a package — not as a floor we're announcing today, but as the direction we're willing to discuss. That package is conditional on three things, and we need to make real progress on all three this round, not just the first: first, FTA/TCA disapplication stands as a general principle tied to the non-market-economy rationale — we can discuss a transitional phase-in period as a goodwill gesture on timing, but not a permanent carve-out or reversal; second, we need actual figures now on how EU-origin steel is currently treated under your safeguard quota allocations — this can't remain a deferred question if you want movement from us on volume and rate; third, we want to work through enforcement and anti-circumvention text — origin verification, licensing conditions — in parallel starting this round, since that's what makes a country-specific model workable for us at all. We're ready to get into detail on all three now.

public_message: We hear the movement, and we want to keep this converging rather than restate positions. Let's be concrete: we can move from our opening figures to a total pool of 800,000 tonnes, with a UK-specific tranche of 400,000 tonnes, an out-of-quota rate of 32%, and a two-year review clause tied to the parallel safeguard processes. That's real movement on our side from where we started, and it sits within the direction you've just described - a country-specific model, a rate moving down from 50, a pool above 400,000. On your three points: first, on FTA/TCA disapplication, 'general principle with a transitional phase-in' isn't yet something we can accept as the final answer, but it's a basis to work from - we'd want that phase-in to run at least three to four years and to be paired with a carve-out for one or two lines where UK production is most concentrated, hot-rolled coil in particular. That combination, not the general-principle framing alone, is what would let us treat this as resolved rather than parked. Second, on EU-origin treatment under our own safeguard measure, we can confirm now that EU allocations under our current safeguard are not being eroded, and we are prepared to consider a modest improvement to the EU's country-specific share there as part of an overall landing - but that is contingent on getting a firm tranche and rate from you here first, not a free-standing offer. Third, on enforcement and anti-circumvention, agreed - let's start on origin verification and licensing conditions in parallel from this round, since that's shared ground regardless of where volume and allocation land, and it strengthens the case for the structured model you're now describing over pure FCFS. We're not asking you to name a floor today, but we do need your actual tranche and rate numbers next round, not another range, if we're going to land this by June.

report: Round 3 at the table: we explicitly rejected the UK's 1,000,000t/500-600k tranche anchor as unworkable against Turkey/Korea's larger volumes and parallel claims, while indicating direction of movement — a country-specific model with a UK tranche 'in the low hundreds of thousands,' a pool above 400,000t but well short of their ask, and a rate moving from 50% toward high-30s/low-40s — conditional on three things: FTA/TCA disapplication standing as a general principle (transitional phase-in on timing only, not reversal or carve-out), actual reciprocity figures on EU treatment under the UK's own safeguard, and parallel work on enforcement/anti-circumvention text. The UK responded with concrete movement: total pool 800,000t, UK-specific tranche 400,000t, out-of-quota rate 32%, two-year review clause — still above our authorised ceiling on every metric (our max is 600k total/220k tranche/38% floor) but a real narrowing from their opening bid. On TCA, they did not accept 'general principle plus phase-in' as sufficient: they want a 3-4 year phase-in AND a permanent-type carve-out for one or two lines, hot-rolled coil specifically — this goes beyond what we're authorised to concede, which is timing flexibility only, not line carve-outs. On reciprocity, they gave a qualitative assurance ('EU allocations are not being eroded') and floated a 'modest improvement' to the EU's share under their safeguard, but explicitly made this contingent on us naming our tranche/rate first, and gave no actual figures despite our direct request. They agreed unconditionally to start parallel work on enforcement/anti-circumvention text. They closed by pressing us to name actual numbers next round rather than another range.

recommendation.reasoning: The UK has moved substantially from its opening anchor but remains above our authorised ceiling on pool size, tranche, and rate, and is asking for more than authorised on TCA (a line-specific carve-out for HRC, not just a phase-in on timing). Crucially, they still have not delivered actual reciprocity figures despite two rounds of us asking directly — their 'modest improvement, contingent on your numbers first' is a negotiating tactic to extract our final position without giving anything verifiable in return. With only one round left, we should not simply hold the range indefinitely, but we also should not move to our ceiling without first securing the reciprocity data and closing off the HRC carve-out ask, since both were explicit preconditions Brussels attached to any further movement. I recommend using round 4 to table our real numbers as a conditional package — but only if the UK delivers actual reciprocity figures at the outset of that round and drops the line-specific carve-out demand in favour of a time-limited phase-in only. If they do not, we should hold at the wider range and let the round close without settlement, preserving the option to proceed with the notified measure while making clear the door remains open given the UK's evident willingness to converge.

instruction: This is the final round, so table our ceiling as a real, final package rather than another range: total TRQ pool of 600,000 tonnes, country-specific UK tranche of 220,000 tonnes, out-of-quota rate of 38%, duration of 3 years with a review at year 2, and parallel agreement on enforcement/anti-circumvention text (origin verification, licensing conditions) as part of the same package. On reciprocity: tell them a qualitative assurance ('not being eroded') plus a vague 'modest improvement' is not sufficient — we need a specific, quantified commitment now on how the EU's country-specific share under their safeguard will be treated (an actual tonnage or percentage figure), as a precondition for us finalising at these numbers. Frame this explicitly as our landing zone: if the UK accepts 600k/220k/38%/3yr-with-2yr-review, a 12-month phase-in only (no HRC carve-out), and puts a real number on reciprocity, we close today. If they hold at 800k/400k/32% or continue to withhold quantified reciprocity or insist on the HRC carve-out, do not move beyond this ceiling — hold firm, and let the round close without settlement rather than authorise further concessions. Do not table anything above this ceiling under any circumstances, and do not let the UK bank the enforcement/anti-circumvention agreement as a standalone concession without the reciprocity figure and TCA terms landing alongside it.

authority.notes: This is the EU's final authorised ceiling for this negotiation: 600,000t total pool, 220,000t UK-specific tranche, 38% out-of-quota rate (hard floor, do not go below), 3-year duration with review at year 2. FTA/TCA disapplication: general principle stands; a transitional phase-in of up to 12 months is the maximum flexibility available; a permanent carve-out or any line-specific exception (including hot-rolled coil) is not authorised under any circumstances and must be stated as a hard no. Finalising at these figures is conditional on the UK providing a specific, quantified reciprocity commitment on treatment of the EU's share under the UK's own safeguard measure — a qualitative assurance is not sufficient. Enforcement/anti-circumvention text (origin verification, licensing conditions) is to be agreed in parallel as part of the same package, not banked separately. If the UK will not meet the reciprocity and TCA conditions, do not exceed this ceiling; allow the round to close without settlement and preserve the default outcome (50%/400,000t global FCFS/no review) as notified.

report: EU has now moved off pure process-talk into indicative numbers. They rejected our 1,000,000t/500-600,000t tranche outright as unworkable against Turkey/Korea's parallel claims, but for the first time floated a substantive direction: a country-specific UK tranche 'in the low hundreds of thousands of tonnes' within a total pool 'larger than 400,000 but well short of' our ask, and an out-of-quota rate moving from 50% toward 'high 30s or low 40s' — explicitly framed as a direction, not a floor. We countered with a concrete bridging offer: 800,000t total pool, 400,000t UK tranche, 32% out-of-quota rate, two-year review clause — real movement from our opening figures, explicitly anchored within the range the EU itself described. report: Round 4 concluded with both sides tabling final, named figures rather than ranges. The two positions remain apart on every quantitative metric: pool (600k v 700k), tranche (220k v 275k), rate (38% v 35%), and materially on phase-in (12 months v 48 months). This is a real, substantive gap, not a rounding difference, and it triggers all three 'do not settle' conditions London set: tranche below 275,000t, rate above 35%, and no meaningful movement on TCA treatment.
